input:
---
title: Debugging
description: Debug failing workflows with snapshots, traces, and the visual inspector.
icon: bug
---

When a workflow fails, Playwriter gives you several tools to understand what went wrong.

## Error snapshots

When an action fails, Playwriter automatically captures a snapshot of the page state at the moment of failure.

```text error output wrap
ActionError: locator('aria-ref=e12') - element not found
  Snapshot at failure:
  [e1] button "Menu" (32x32 at 16,16)
  [e2] link "Home" (48x20 at 80,18)
  ...no element with ref e12 found
```

## Trace viewer

Record a trace of every action, network request, and console log.

```bash
playwriter -s 1 --trace -e "
  page.goto('https://example.com')
  page.locator('text=Login').click()
  page.locator('#email').fill('user@test.com')
"
```

The trace file can be opened in Playwright's trace viewer:

```bash
npx playwright show-trace trace.zip
```

## Console logs

Forward browser console output to the terminal.

```ts
page.on('console', (msg) => console.log(`[browser] ${msg.type()}: ${msg.text()}`))
```

## Network failures

Listen for failed network requests to catch API errors.

```ts
page.on('requestfailed', (req) => {
  console.error(`Failed: ${req.method()} ${req.url()} - ${req.failure()?.errorText}`)
})
```

## Page crashes

Detect and handle page crashes gracefully.

```ts
page.on('crash', () => {
  console.error('Page crashed! Taking recovery snapshot...')
})
```

## Step-by-step execution

Add `pause()` calls to stop execution and inspect page state interactively.

```ts
await page.goto('https://example.com')
await page.pause() // opens the Playwright inspector
await page.locator('text=Submit').click()
```

name: example/src/deployment.mdx
input:
---
title: Deployment
description: Deploy your docs with one command. Preview every branch automatically.
icon: cloud-upload
iconColor: orange
---

# Deployment

Holocron deploys your documentation site to **holocron.so** with a single command. Every deploy gets a live URL.

```bash
npx -y "@holocron.so/cli" deploy
```

The deploy command runs `vite build`, collects the output, and uploads it. Files are content-addressed (SHA-256 hashed), so unchanged files are never re-uploaded. A typical redeploy after a small edit uploads only the changed pages.

## GitHub Actions

The recommended way to deploy is from GitHub Actions. Add this workflow to your repo:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read
  deployments: write

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: holocron
      url: ${{ steps.deploy.outputs.holocron_url }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: oven-sh/setup-bun@v2
      - run: bun install
      - name: Deploy
        id: deploy
        run: npx -y "@holocron.so/cli" deploy
        env:
          HOLOCRON_KEY: ${{ secrets.HOLOCRON_KEY }}
```

<Aside>

<Info>
The `environment` block makes the deployed URL clickable as a **deployment status** on every commit and PR in GitHub's UI.
</Info>

</Aside>

**What each section does:**

- `permissions: id-token: write` enables keyless OIDC authentication (see below).
- `environment.url` reads the deploy URL from a step output, so GitHub shows it inline.
- `HOLOCRON_KEY` is optional if OIDC is configured. It serves as a fallback or explicit override.

### Step outputs

The deploy command automatically sets two GitHub Actions step outputs:

| Output                   | Description                     |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------- |
| `holocron_url`           | The live URL of the deployment  |
| `holocron_deployment_id` | The deployment ID for API calls |

Use them in downstream steps, for example to post a comment with the deployment link:

```yaml
- name: Comment deployment URL
  if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
  run: |
    gh pr comment ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} \
      --body "Preview: ${{ steps.deploy.outputs.holocron_url }}"
  env:
    GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
```

## Keyless deploys (OIDC)

If you've signed in to [holocron.so](https://holocron.so) with your GitHub account, deployments from GitHub Actions **don't need any secrets**. The Vite plugin detects the GitHub Actions environment during `vite build` and authenticates via [OpenID Connect](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/security-hardening-your-deployments/about-security-hardening-with-openid-connect).

**How it works:**

1. GitHub Actions mints a short-lived JWT containing your repo name, branch, and actor ID.
2. The Vite plugin sends this token to `holocron.so` during the build step.
3. The server verifies the JWT against GitHub's public keys, matches the actor to your holocron account, and returns a project-scoped API key.
4. The deploy command uses that key for the rest of the upload.

**Prerequisites:**

- Sign in to [holocron.so](https://holocron.so) with the GitHub account that owns the repo (or has push access).
- Set `permissions: id-token: write` in your workflow.

No `HOLOCRON_KEY` secret is needed. If both OIDC and `HOLOCRON_KEY` are available, the explicit key takes priority.

## Deployment URLs

When deploying from **GitHub Actions** (OIDC), your site URL is derived from the
verified GitHub **repo name** and **owner**:

```txt
https://<repo>-<owner>-site.holocron.so
```

Pushing to the default branch (usually `main`) updates the production URL.
Pushing to any other branch or opening a pull request creates a unique preview
URL that includes the branch name. The deploy command prints the URL and sets it
as the `holocron_url` step output.

When deploying **locally** or with an **API key**, the URL uses the project ID
instead (`https://<projectId>-site.holocron.so`).

## Branch detection

The branch name is detected automatically:

- **Pull requests:** `GITHUB_HEAD_REF` (the source branch, e.g. `fix-typo`)
- **Pushes:** `GITHUB_REF` stripped to the branch name (e.g. `refs/heads/main` → `main`)
- **Explicit override:** `--branch <name>` flag on the deploy command

## Using an API key

For CI systems other than GitHub Actions, or if you prefer explicit authentication, create an API key and pass it as `HOLOCRON_KEY`:

```bash
# Create a key (requires login)
npx -y "@holocron.so/cli" keys create --name production --project <projectId>

# Deploy with the key
HOLOCRON_KEY=holo_xxx npx -y "@holocron.so/cli" deploy
```

In GitHub Actions, store the key as a [repository secret](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/using-secrets-in-github-actions) and reference it with `${{ secrets.HOLOCRON_KEY }}`.

## CLI options

```bash
npx -y "@holocron.so/cli" deploy [options]
```

| Option            | Description                                                         |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--branch <name>` | Override the branch name for deployment metadata                    |
| `--project <id>`  | Project ID (only needed with session auth, not with `HOLOCRON_KEY`) |
| `--skip-build`    | Skip the `vite build` step and upload the existing `dist/`          |

## Self-hosting

If you prefer to host the site yourself, `vite build` produces a standalone server you can run anywhere.

### Node.js

```bash
npx vite build
node dist/rsc/index.js
```

The server listens on port **3000** by default. Set the `PORT` environment variable to change it. Place a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy) in front for TLS and domain routing.

### Docker

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./
RUN corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
COPY . .
RUN pnpm build
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/rsc/index.js"]
```

### Cloudflare Workers

Install the Cloudflare Vite plugin:

```bash
pnpm add -D wrangler @cloudflare/vite-plugin
```

Update `vite.config.ts`:

```ts
import { cloudflare } from '@cloudflare/vite-plugin'
import { holocron } from '@holocron.so/vite'
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    holocron(),
    cloudflare({
      viteEnvironment: {
        name: 'rsc',
        childEnvironments: ['ssr'],
      },
    }),
  ],
})
```

Create a `wrangler.jsonc`:

```jsonc
{
  "name": "my-docs",
  "main": "spiceflow/cloudflare-entrypoint",
  "compatibility_date": "2026-04-14",
  "compatibility_flags": ["nodejs_compat"]
}
```

Build and deploy:

```bash
npx vite build
npx wrangler deploy
```

### Environment variables

| Variable | Default | Description                       |
| -------- | ------- | --------------------------------- |
| `PORT`   | 3000    | Server listen port (Node.js only) |

name: example/src/frontmatter.mdx
input:
---
title: Frontmatter
description: Page-level metadata you can set in YAML frontmatter at the top of any MDX file.
icon: file-text
---

Every MDX page can include a YAML frontmatter block at the top. Frontmatter controls the page title, sidebar appearance, SEO tags, and other per-page behavior.

```yaml
---
$schema: https://holocron.so/frontmatter.json
title: Getting Started
description: Learn how to set up your first project.
icon: rocket
---
```

## Core fields

**`title`** sets the page title used in the sidebar, browser tab, and `<h1>` heading. If omitted, Holocron falls back to the first heading in the MDX body, then `"Untitled"`.

**`description`** sets the page description used in the `<meta name="description">` tag and OpenGraph metadata. Falls back to the site-level description from `docs.json` if not set.

**`icon`** sets an icon displayed next to the page title in the sidebar. Uses the icon library configured in `docs.json` (Font Awesome by default, or Lucide). You can also use the full `library:name` format like `fontawesome:brands:discord`.

```yaml
---
$schema: https://holocron.so/frontmatter.json
title: Authentication
description: Learn how to authenticate API requests.
icon: lock
---
```

## Sidebar fields

**`sidebarTitle`** overrides the title shown in the sidebar navigation. Useful when the full title is too long for the sidebar but you want it as the page heading.

**`tag`** adds a small badge next to the page title in the sidebar. Common values are `BETA`, `NEW`, `PREVIEW`. The tag only shows when `api` is not set.

**`deprecated`** adds a `Deprecated` badge next to the page in the sidebar when set to `true`.

**`api`** is a Mintlify convention for API reference pages. Set it to an HTTP method and path like `"GET /users"`. The HTTP method (`GET`, `POST`, etc.) renders as a colored badge in the sidebar.

```yaml
---
$schema: https://holocron.so/frontmatter.json
title: List Users
api: GET /users
---
```

```yaml
---
$schema: https://holocron.so/frontmatter.json
title: Sidebar Override
sidebarTitle: Short Name
tag: BETA
deprecated: true
---
```

## Page layout mode

**`mode`** controls the page layout. It is Mintlify-compatible and accepts `default`, `wide`, `center`, `custom`, or `frame`. Holocron keeps the layout system small and collapses these five values into two layouts.

| `mode`    | Left navigation sidebar | Aliases to |
| --------- | ----------------------- | ---------- |
| `default` | shown                   | —          |
| `wide`    | shown                   | `default`  |
| `frame`   | shown                   | `default`  |
| `center`  | **hidden**              | —          |
| `custom`  | **hidden**              | `center`   |

The `center` layout hides the left navigation sidebar and centers the content within the page width. Use it for landing pages, changelogs, or any page where you want the focus on the content instead of the navigation chrome.

```yaml
---
$schema: https://holocron.so/frontmatter.json
title: Changelog
mode: center
---
```

<Note>
Holocron only implements two real layouts (`default` and `center`). The other Mintlify mode names are accepted so existing `docs.json` projects validate without changes, but `wide` and `frame` alias to `default`, and `custom` aliases to `center`.
</Note>

## Visibility and indexing

**`hidden`** hides the page from the sidebar navigation and adds a `noindex` robots meta tag. The page is still routable by its URL.

**`noindex`** adds a `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` tag but keeps the page visible in the sidebar. Use this for pages that should be accessible but not indexed by search engines.

**`robots`** sets a custom `<meta name="robots">` value. Overrides the default behavior. Common values: `noindex`, `noarchive`, `nofollow`.

```yaml
---
$schema: https://holocron.so/frontmatter.json
title: Internal Guide
hidden: true
---
```

```yaml
---
$schema: https://holocron.so/frontmatter.json
title: Draft Page
noindex: true
---
```

## SEO and keywords

**`keywords`** is an array of strings rendered as a `<meta name="keywords">` tag. Keywords also boost the page in Holocron's built-in sidebar search.

```yaml
---
$schema: https://holocron.so/frontmatter.json
title: Configuration
keywords: ["setup", "config", "options"]
---
```

## OpenGraph metadata

Override the default OpenGraph tags for social sharing previews. These are rendered as `<meta property="og:...">` tags in the page `<head>`.

| Field             | Description                                                  |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `og:title`        | Social share title. Defaults to `{title} — {siteName}`.      |
| `og:description`  | Social share description. Defaults to page `description`.    |
| `og:image`        | Social share image URL. Defaults to auto-generated OG image. |
| `og:url`          | Canonical URL for the page.                                  |
| `og:type`         | OpenGraph type, e.g. `article`.                              |
| `og:image:width`  | Image width in pixels (string or number).                    |
| `og:image:height` | Image height in pixels (string or number).                   |

```yaml
---
$schema: https://holocron.so/frontmatter.json
title: API Overview
"og:title": Custom Social Title
"og:description": A custom description for social cards.
"og:image": https://example.com/og.png
"og:image:width": 1200
"og:image:height": 630
---
```

## Twitter/X metadata

Override the default Twitter Card tags. These are rendered as `<meta name="twitter:...">` tags.

| Field                  | Description                                              |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `twitter:title`        | Twitter card title. Defaults to `og:title`.              |
| `twitter:description`  | Twitter card description. Defaults to `og:description`.  |
| `twitter:image`        | Twitter card image. Defaults to `og:image`.              |
| `twitter:card`         | Card type: `summary` or `summary_large_image` (default). |
| `twitter:site`         | Twitter handle for the site, e.g. `@mycompany`.          |
| `twitter:image:width`  | Image width in pixels (string or number).                |
| `twitter:image:height` | Image height in pixels (string or number).               |

```yaml
---
$schema: https://holocron.so/frontmatter.json
"twitter:card": summary
"twitter:site": "@mycompany"
"twitter:image": https://example.com/twitter.png
---
```

## Rendering strategy

**`rendering`** controls how the page is rendered. It accepts `ssr` (the default) or `static`.

With `ssr`, the page is rendered on every request, so it can react to per-request data like cookies. With `static`, the page is **prerendered to static HTML at build time** for faster delivery and cheaper hosting. Use `static` only for pages whose content never depends on the incoming request.

```yaml
---
$schema: https://holocron.so/frontmatter.json
title: Changelog
rendering: static
---
```

## Advanced fields

**`gridGap`** overrides the horizontal gap (in pixels) between the content column and sidebars for this page only. The default is `60`. OpenAPI pages use `30` automatically.

**`cache-control`** sets a custom `Cache-Control` header on the page response. Defaults to `s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=86400`. Set to `s-maxage=0, no-store` to disable caching entirely.

```yaml
---
$schema: https://holocron.so/frontmatter.json
title: Real-time Dashboard
cache-control: "s-maxage=0, no-store"
gridGap: 40
---
```

## Passthrough

The frontmatter schema uses `.passthrough()`, so any additional YAML fields you add are preserved and accessible in the parsed frontmatter object. This is useful for custom metadata consumed by your own components or plugins.

```yaml
---
$schema: https://holocron.so/frontmatter.json
title: Custom Page
myCustomField: hello
myList:
  - one
  - two
---
```

--- title: Playwriter description: CLI & MCP for agent browser automation icon: home ---

playwriter

CLI & MCP for agent browser automation
If you like **Playwriter** please [star on GitHub](https://github.com/remorses/playwriter). It helps give more visibility to the project!
A Chrome extension that let your agents control **your actual browser** — with logins, extensions, and cookies already there. No headless instance, no bot detection, no extra memory. *Your existing Chrome session. Extensions, logins, cookies — all there.* Other browser MCPs either **spawn a fresh Chrome** or give agents a fixed set of tools. New Chrome means no logins, no extensions, instant bot detection, and double the memory. Fixed tools mean the agent can't profile performance, can't set breakpoints, can't intercept network requests — it can only do what someone decided to expose. Playwriter gives agents the **full Playwright API** through a single `execute` tool. One tool, any Playwright code, no wrappers. Low context usage because there's no schema bloat from dozens of tool definitions. And it runs in your existing browser, so **nothing extra gets spawned**. ## Trusted by developers everywhere Marquee with logo images (SVG): Marquee with icons: ## Blockquote > Playwriter changed the way I think about browser automation. It's not just a tool, > it's a paradigm shift for how agents interact with the web. ## The `execute` tool One tool to rule them all. Pass any Playwright code and it runs in your browser. ```ts title="automate.ts" import { chromium } from 'playwright' async function automateWorkflow() { const browser = await chromium.connectOverCDP('http://localhost:9222') const context = browser.contexts()[0] const page = context.pages()[0] // Navigate and wait for network idle await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard', { waitUntil: 'networkidle', }) // Fill in the search form const searchInput = page.locator('[data-testid="search-input"]') await searchInput.fill('quarterly report') await searchInput.press('Enter') // Wait for results and extract data await page.waitForSelector('.results-table tbody tr') const rows = await page.$$eval('.results-table tbody tr', (trs) => trs.map((tr) => ({ title: tr.querySelector('td:nth-child(1)')?.textContent?.trim(), date: tr.querySelector('td:nth-child(2)')?.textContent?.trim(), status: tr.querySelector('td:nth-child(3)')?.textContent?.trim(), })), ) console.log(`Found ${rows.length} results`) for (const row of rows) { console.log(` ${row.title} — ${row.date} — ${row.status}`) } // Click the first result and download await page.locator('.results-table tbody tr:first-child a').click() const [download] = await Promise.all([ page.waitForEvent('download'), page.locator('button:has-text("Export PDF")').click(), ]) const path = await download.path() console.log(`Downloaded to: ${path}`) } automateWorkflow() ``` Here's another example without full bleed (default `bleed-right`): ```ts title="scraper.ts" import { chromium } from 'playwright' async function scrapeData() { const browser = await chromium.connectOverCDP('http://localhost:9222') const context = browser.contexts()[0] const page = context.pages()[0] await page.goto('https://news.example.com') const articles = await page.$$eval('article', (els) => els.map((el) => ({ title: el.querySelector('h2')?.textContent, link: el.querySelector('a')?.href, summary: el.querySelector('p')?.textContent, })), ) return articles.filter((a) => a.title) } scrapeData().then(console.log) ``` ## Getting started **Four steps** and your agent is browsing.
**Requirements:** Chrome or Chromium installed, Node.js 18+, and a Playwriter-compatible agent (OpenCode, Cursor, Claude Code, etc).
### Install the extension 1. Install the [Chrome extension](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/playwriter-mcp/jfeammnjpkecdekppnclgkkffahnhfhe) 2. Click the extension icon on a tab — it turns green ### Install CLI + skill Install the CLI, then add the skill so your agent knows the good Playwriter workflows. ```bash bleed=true npm i -g playwriter ``` Then install the **skill** — it teaches your agent how to use Playwriter: which selectors to use, how to avoid timeouts, how to read snapshots, and all available utilities. ```bash bleed=true npx -y skills add remorses/playwriter -g -y ``` #### First commands The extension connects your browser to a **local WebSocket relay** on `localhost:19988`. The CLI sends Playwright code through the relay. No remote servers, no accounts, nothing leaves your machine. ```bash playwriter session new # new sandbox, outputs id (e.g. 1) playwriter -e "page.goto('https://example.com')" playwriter -e "snapshot({ page })" playwriter -e "page.locator('aria-ref=e5').click()" ``` *Extension icon green = connected. Gray = not attached to this tab.* ```text Wrapped prompt wrap Use the Playwriter skill. I have a remote browser session open at --session remote-debug and I want you to snapshot the page, test selectors, and execute code against the live browser without restarting the workflow. ``` ## Using `chrome.debugger` API Click the extension icon on a tab — it attaches via `chrome.debugger` and opens a WebSocket to a local relay. Your agent (CLI, MCP, or a Playwright script) connects to the same relay. **CDP commands flow through**; the extension forwards them to Chrome and sends responses back. No Chrome restart, no flags, no special setup. ```diagram ┌───────────────────────┐ WebSocket ┌──────────────────────┐ │ Chrome tab │<─────────────────────>│ Local relay :19988 │ │ extension enabled │ │ /extension + /cdp/id │ └───────────┬───────────┘ └──────────┬───────────┘ │ chrome.debugger │ Playwright CDP v v Page DOM, network, JS CLI, MCP, agents ``` The relay **multiplexes sessions**, so multiple agents or CLI instances can work with the same browser at the same time. ## Collaboration Because the agent works in **your browser**, you can collaborate. You see everything it does in real time. When it hits a captcha, **you solve it**. When a consent wall appears, you click through it. When the agent gets stuck, you disable the extension on that tab, fix things manually, re-enable it, and the agent picks up where it left off. You're not watching a remote screen or reading logs after the fact. You're **sharing a browser** — the agent does the repetitive work, you step in when it needs a human. ## Accessibility snapshots
Snapshots are the **primary way** agents read pages. Only use screenshots when spatial layout matters (grids, dashboards, maps).
Your agent needs to **see the page** before it can act. Accessibility snapshots return every interactive element as text, with Playwright locators attached. **5–20KB instead of 100KB+** for a screenshot — cheaper, faster, and the agent can parse them without vision. ```bash playwriter -e "snapshot({ page })" # Output: # - banner: # - link "Home" [id="nav-home"] # - navigation: # - link "Docs" [data-testid="docs-link"] # - link "Blog" role=link[name="Blog"] ``` ### Search and diff Each line ends with a **locator** you can pass directly to `page.locator()`. Subsequent calls return a **diff**, so you only see what changed. Use `search` to filter large pages. ```bash # Search for specific elements playwriter -e "snapshot({ page, search: /button|submit/i })" # Always print URL first, then snapshot — pages can redirect playwriter -e "console.log('URL:', page.url()); snapshot({ page }).then(console.log)" ``` Use snapshots as the **primary way to read pages**. Only reach for screenshots when spatial layout matters — grids, dashboards, maps. ## Visual labels When the agent needs to understand **where things are on screen**, `screenshotWithAccessibilityLabels` overlays **Vimium-style labels** on every interactive element. The agent sees the screenshot, reads the labels, and clicks by reference. ```bash playwriter -e "screenshotWithAccessibilityLabels({ page })" # Returns screenshot + accessibility snapshot with aria-ref selectors playwriter -e "page.locator('aria-ref=e5').click()" ``` Labels are **color-coded by element type**: yellow for links, orange for buttons, coral for inputs, pink for checkboxes, peach for sliders, salmon for menus, amber for tabs. The ref system is shared with `snapshot()`, so you can switch between text and visual modes freely. *Vimium-style labels. Screenshot + snapshot in one call.* ## Sessions ### Isolated state Run **multiple agents at once** without them stepping on each other. Each session is an isolated sandbox with its own `state` object. Variables, pages, and listeners persist between calls. Browser tabs are shared, but state is not. ```bash playwriter session new # => 1 playwriter session new # => 2 playwriter session list # shows sessions + state keys # Session 1 stores data playwriter -s 1 -e "state.users = page.$$eval('.user', els => els.map(e => e.textContent))" # Session 2 can't see it playwriter -s 2 -e "console.log(state.users)" # undefined ``` ### Dedicated pages Create your own page to **avoid interference** from other agents. Reuse an existing `about:blank` tab or create a fresh one, and store it in `state`. ```bash playwriter -s 1 -e "state.myPage = context.pages().find(p => p.url() === 'about:blank') ?? context.newPage(); state.myPage.goto('https://example.com')" # All subsequent calls use state.myPage playwriter -s 1 -e "state.myPage.title()" ``` ## Debugger & editor Things no other browser MCP can do. **Set breakpoints**, step through code, inspect variables at runtime. **Live-edit page scripts and CSS** without reloading. Full Chrome DevTools Protocol access, not a watered-down subset. ```bash # Set breakpoints and debug playwriter -e "state.cdp = getCDPSession({ page }); state.dbg = createDebugger({ cdp: state.cdp }); state.dbg.enable()" playwriter -e "state.scripts = state.dbg.listScripts({ search: 'app' }); state.scripts.map(s => s.url)" playwriter -e "state.dbg.setBreakpoint({ file: state.scripts[0].url, line: 42 })" # Live edit page code playwriter -e "state.editor = createEditor({ cdp: state.cdp }); state.editor.enable()" playwriter -e "state.editor.edit({ url: 'https://example.com/app.js', oldString: 'const DEBUG = false', newString: 'const DEBUG = true' })" ``` Edits are **in-memory** and persist until the page reloads. Useful for toggling debug flags, patching broken code, or testing quick fixes without touching source files. The editor also supports `grep` across all loaded scripts. *Breakpoints, stepping, variable inspection — from the CLI.* ## Network interception Let the agent **watch network traffic** to reverse-engineer APIs, scrape data behind JavaScript rendering, or debug failing requests. Captured data lives in `state` and persists across calls. ```bash # Start intercepting playwriter -e "state.responses = []; page.on('response', async res => { if (res.url().includes('/api/')) { try { state.responses.push({ url: res.url(), status: res.status(), body: await res.json() }); } catch {} } })" # Trigger actions, then analyze playwriter -e "page.click('button.load-more')" playwriter -e "console.log('Captured', state.responses.length, 'API calls'); state.responses.forEach(r => console.log(r.status, r.url.slice(0, 80)))" # Replay an API call directly playwriter -e "page.evaluate(async (url) => { const res = await fetch(url); return res.json(); }, state.responses[0].url)" ``` **Faster than scraping the DOM.** The agent captures the real API calls, inspects their schemas, and replays them with different parameters. Works for pagination, authenticated endpoints, and anything behind client-side rendering. ## Screen recording Have the agent **record what it's doing** as MP4 video. The recording uses `chrome.tabCapture` and runs in the extension context, so it **survives page navigation**. ```bash # Start recording playwriter -e "startRecording({ page, outputPath: './recording.mp4', frameRate: 30 })" # Navigate, interact — recording continues playwriter -e "page.click('a'); page.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded')" playwriter -e "page.goBack()" # Stop and save playwriter -e "stopRecording({ page })" ``` Unlike `getDisplayMedia`, this approach **persists across navigations** because the extension holds the `MediaRecorder`, not the page. You can also check recording status with `isRecording` or cancel without saving with `cancelRecording`. *Native tab capture. 30–60fps. Survives navigation.* ## Comparison Why use this over the alternatives. ### vs Playwright MCP | Feature | Playwright MCP | Playwriter | | ------------- | ----------------- | -------------------- | | Browser | Spawns new Chrome | Uses your Chrome | | Extensions | None | Your existing ones | | Login state | Fresh | Already logged in | | Bot detection | Always detected | Can bypass | | Collaboration | Separate window | Same browser as user | ### vs Playwright CLI | Feature | Playwright CLI | Playwriter | | --------------- | ------------------- | ----------------------------- | | Browser | Spawns new browser | Uses your Chrome | | Login state | Fresh | Already logged in | | Extensions | None | Your existing ones | | Captchas | Always blocked | Bypass (disconnect extension) | | Collaboration | Separate window | Same browser as user | | Capabilities | Limited command set | Anything Playwright can do | | Raw CDP access | No | Yes | | Video recording | File-based tracing | Native tab capture (30–60fps) | ### vs BrowserMCP | Feature | BrowserMCP | Playwriter | | ------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------ | | Tools | 12+ dedicated tools | 1 execute tool | | API | Limited actions | Full Playwright | | Context usage | High (tool schemas) | Low | | LLM knowledge | Must learn tools | Already knows Playwright | ### vs Claude Browser Extension | Feature | Claude Extension | Playwriter | | -------------------- | -------------------- | ----------------------- | | Agent support | Claude only | Any MCP client | | Windows WSL | No | Yes | | Context method | Screenshots (100KB+) | A11y snapshots (5–20KB) | | Playwright API | No | Full | | Debugger | No | Yes | | Live code editing | No | Yes | | Network interception | Limited | Full | | Raw CDP access | No | Yes | ### vs Built-in Chrome CDP (`--remote-debugging-port`) | Feature | Built-in CDP | Playwriter | | ------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | | Setup | Restart Chrome with special flags | Click extension icon | | Confirmation dialog | Automation infobar agents can't dismiss | No blocking dialog | | Autonomous agents | Interrupted by debug banners | Fully autonomous | | User disruption | Banners appear mid-workflow | Silent — no interruption | | Existing session | Must relaunch Chrome (lose state) | Uses your running browser | ## Remote access ### Tunnel Control Chrome on a **remote machine** — a headless Mac mini, a cloud VM, a devcontainer. A [traforo](https://traforo.dev) tunnel exposes the relay through Cloudflare. **No VPN, no firewall rules, no port forwarding.** ```bash # On the host machine — start relay with tunnel npx -y traforo -p 19988 -t my-machine -- npx -y playwriter serve --token # From anywhere — set env vars and use normally export PLAYWRITER_HOST=https://my-machine-tunnel.traforo.dev export PLAYWRITER_TOKEN= playwriter -e "page.goto('https://example.com')" ``` ### LAN Also works on a **LAN without tunnels** — just set `PLAYWRITER_HOST=192.168.1.10`. Works for MCP too — set `PLAYWRITER_HOST` and `PLAYWRITER_TOKEN` in your MCP client env config. Use cases: headless Mac mini, remote user support, multi-machine automation, dev from a VM or devcontainer. ## Security Everything runs **on your machine**. The relay binds to `localhost:19988` and only accepts connections from the extension. No remote server, no account, no telemetry. - **Local only** — WebSocket server binds to localhost. Nothing leaves your machine. - **Origin validation** — only the Playwriter extension origin is accepted. Browsers cannot spoof the Origin header, so malicious websites cannot connect. - **Explicit consent** — only tabs where you clicked the extension icon are controlled. No background access. - **Visible automation** — Chrome shows an automation banner on controlled tabs. ## Authentication flows Playwriter excels at automating login flows because it uses your real browser with existing cookies and sessions. When an agent needs to interact with authenticated pages, it simply inherits whatever login state already exists in Chrome. For multi-account workflows, create separate Chrome profiles and connect each to a different Playwriter session. The extension manages CDP connections per-profile. ```ts // already logged into GitHub in this Chrome profile await page.goto('https://github.com/settings/profile') const name = await page.locator('#user_profile_name').inputValue() console.log('Logged in as:', name) ``` ## Form filling Playwriter handles all HTML form elements: text inputs, selects, checkboxes, radio buttons, file uploads, date pickers, and rich text editors. ```ts await page.locator('#name').fill('Jane Doe') await page.locator('select#country').selectOption('US') await page.locator('input[type=checkbox]#terms').check() await page.locator('input[type=file]').setInputFiles('/tmp/resume.pdf') ``` For date pickers implemented as custom widgets (not native ``), use the calendar UI through click sequences or inject the value directly. ## Keyboard shortcuts Send keyboard shortcuts to trigger app actions that have no clickable button. ```ts await page.keyboard.press('Control+Shift+P') // open command palette await page.keyboard.type('format document') await page.keyboard.press('Enter') ``` Modifier keys: `Control`, `Shift`, `Alt`, `Meta` (Cmd on macOS). ## Mouse interactions Beyond clicks, Playwriter supports hover, drag-and-drop, and scroll gestures. ```ts // hover to reveal a tooltip await page.locator('.info-icon').hover() // drag and drop await page.locator('#item-3').dragTo(page.locator('#dropzone')) // scroll to bottom await page.mouse.wheel(0, 10000) ``` ## File downloads Intercept and save file downloads triggered by clicking export buttons or download links. ```ts const downloadPromise = page.waitForEvent('download') await page.locator('text=Export CSV').click() const download = await downloadPromise await download.saveAs('/tmp/report.csv') console.log('Downloaded:', download.suggestedFilename()) ``` ## Popup and dialog handling Handle `alert()`, `confirm()`, and `prompt()` dialogs automatically. ```ts page.on('dialog', async (dialog) => { console.log('Dialog:', dialog.type(), dialog.message()) if (dialog.type() === 'confirm') { await dialog.accept() } else { await dialog.dismiss() } }) ``` New tabs opened by `window.open()` are captured as new pages in the same context. ## Multi-tab workflows Some workflows span multiple tabs — OAuth flows, payment redirects, or "open in new tab" links. ```ts const [newPage] = await Promise.all([ context.waitForEvent('page'), page.locator('text=Open settings').click(), // opens new tab ]) await newPage.waitForLoadState() console.log('New tab URL:', newPage.url()) ``` ## Geolocation and permissions Override browser geolocation and permissions for testing location-aware features. ```ts await context.setGeolocation({ latitude: 37.7749, longitude: -122.4194 }) await context.grantPermissions(['geolocation']) await page.goto('https://maps.example.com') ``` ## Mobile emulation Emulate mobile devices for responsive testing. ```ts await page.setViewportSize({ width: 375, height: 812 }) // iPhone X await page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'dark' }) ``` ## Performance metrics Collect Web Vitals and other performance metrics during automation. ```ts const metrics = await page.evaluate(() => { const entries = performance.getEntriesByType('navigation') const nav = entries[0] return { domContentLoaded: nav.domContentLoadedEventEnd, loadComplete: nav.loadEventEnd, transferSize: nav.transferSize, } }) console.log('Page load metrics:', metrics) ``` ## Cookie management Read, set, and clear cookies for session management. ```ts // read all cookies const cookies = await context.cookies() console.log(cookies.map(c => `${c.name}=${c.value}`).join('; ')) // set a cookie await context.addCookies([{ name: 'session', value: 'abc123', domain: '.example.com', path: '/', }]) // clear all cookies await context.clearCookies() ``` ## Local storage Access and modify localStorage for debugging or test setup. ```ts // read const token = await page.evaluate(() => localStorage.getItem('auth_token')) // write await page.evaluate(() => localStorage.setItem('feature_flag', 'true')) // clear await page.evaluate(() => localStorage.clear()) ``` ## Error recovery Build resilient automations that recover from transient failures. ```ts async function withRetry(fn, maxAttempts = 3) { for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) { try { return await fn() } catch (err) { if (attempt === maxAttempts) throw err console.log(`Attempt ${attempt} failed, retrying...`) await page.waitForTimeout(1000 * attempt) } } } await withRetry(async () => { await page.locator('text=Submit').click() await page.waitForResponse('**/api/submit') }) ``` ## Questions Playwriter is a CLI and MCP server that drives your own Chrome through a browser extension. Agents write Playwright code and it runs against your logged-in tabs. Any recent Playwright release works. The `page` object you get is a real Playwright `Page`, so the full API is available: - `page.goto()`, `page.click()`, `page.fill()` - `page.screenshot()` and `page.pdf()` - `page.route()` for network interception Yes. Start the relay on the host machine with a tunnel and point `PLAYWRITER_RELAY_URL` at it from anywhere. See [Remote access](#remote-access). Sessions live in memory on the relay. Nothing is written to disk unless you save a recording or a screenshot.

---
title: Introduction
description: Welcome to Holocron — a Mintlify drop-in replacement as a Vite plugin.
icon: play
iconColor: green
---

## What is Holocron?

Holocron turns your MDX files into a beautiful documentation site. Point your `vite.config.ts` at the plugin and start writing docs.

## Features

- **MDX support** — write documentation in Markdown with embedded JSX components
- **Mintlify compatible** — drop-in replacement for `docs.json` configuration
- **Vite powered** — fast dev server with hot module replacement
- **React Server Components** — zero-JS pages by default, interactive where you need it

## Quick example

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import { holocron } from '@holocron.so/vite'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [holocron()],
})
```

## Callouts

<Note>This adds a note in the content.</Note>

<Warning>This raises a warning to watch out for.</Warning>

<Info>This draws attention to important information.</Info>

<Tip>This suggests a helpful tip.</Tip>

<Check>This brings us a checked status.</Check>

<Danger>This is a danger callout.</Danger>

<Callout color="#FFC107">This is a custom callout with its own color.</Callout>

## Native details

Holocron also supports copied HTML `<details>` blocks and renders them with the same expandable UI.

<details open>
<summary>Show a **rich** summary with a [link](https://holocron.so)</summary>

Details can contain normal markdown content, including tables and code blocks.

| Component | Support |
| --------- | ------- |
| Tables    | Yes     |
| Code      | Yes     |

```ts
import { holocron } from '@holocron.so/vite'

export default {
  plugins: [holocron()],
}
```
</details>

<Aside>

<Callout type="note">Callouts work inside Asides too — no nested frames.</Callout>

</Aside>

input:
---
title: Navigation
description: Organize tabs, groups, and pages for a larger docs site.
---

## Navigation basics

Holocron follows the Mintlify `docs.json` navigation shape closely. Top-level groups become sidebar sections, and pages inside those groups become leaf items or nested trees.

## Grouping content

Use groups to break a larger docs site into clear sections such as onboarding, guides, and reference material.

```json
{
  "navigation": [
    {
      "group": "Getting Started",
      "pages": ["introduction", "quickstart"]
    },
    {
      "group": "Reference",
      "pages": ["configuration", "deployment"]
    }
  ]
}
```

## Tabs and anchors

When a docs site grows further, tabs help split the sidebar into multiple top-level areas while `global.anchors` add external destinations such as GitHub or a changelog.

## Headings in the sidebar

The current page can also expose an `On this page` subtree so readers can move between sections without leaving the main navigation column.

---
title: Network interception
description: Intercept, modify, and mock network requests during automation.
icon: wifi
---

Playwriter can intercept HTTP requests and responses, letting agents mock APIs, block resources, or inspect traffic.

## Intercepting requests

```ts
await page.route('**/api/users', (route) => {
  route.fulfill({
    status: 200,
    contentType: 'application/json',
    body: JSON.stringify([{ id: 1, name: 'Test User' }]),
  })
})
```

## Blocking resources

Speed up page loads by blocking images, fonts, or analytics scripts.

```ts
await page.route('**/*.{png,jpg,gif}', (route) => route.abort())
await page.route('**/analytics/**', (route) => route.abort())
```

## Modifying responses

Transform response bodies before the page receives them.

```ts
await page.route('**/api/config', async (route) => {
  const response = await route.fetch()
  const json = await response.json()
  json.featureFlags.darkMode = true
  route.fulfill({ response, body: JSON.stringify(json) })
})
```

## Recording HAR files

Capture all network traffic to a HAR file for later analysis.

```ts
await page.routeFromHAR('traffic.har', { update: true })
// ... run your workflow ...
await page.close() // HAR is saved on close
```

## Waiting for responses

Wait for a specific API call to complete before proceeding.

```ts
const responsePromise = page.waitForResponse('**/api/submit')
await page.locator('text=Submit').click()
const response = await responsePromise
console.log(response.status(), await response.json())
```

title: Screen recording
description: Capture screenshots and record video during automation sessions.
icon: monitor
---

Playwriter can capture screenshots of the current viewport or full page, and record video of the entire session for debugging.

## Full-page screenshot

```ts
await page.screenshot({ path: '/tmp/full.png', fullPage: true })
```

## Element screenshot

Capture a single element without the surrounding page.

```ts
const card = page.locator('.product-card').first()
await card.screenshot({ path: '/tmp/card.png' })
```

## Clipped region

Capture a specific rectangular area of the viewport.

```ts
await page.screenshot({
  path: '/tmp/header.png',
  clip: { x: 0, y: 0, width: 1440, height: 80 },
})
```

## Video recording

Enable video recording when creating a session.

```ts
const context = await browser.newContext({
  recordVideo: { dir: '/tmp/videos/', size: { width: 1280, height: 720 } },
})
```

## PDF export

Export the current page as a PDF (Chromium only).

```ts
await page.pdf({ path: '/tmp/page.pdf', format: 'A4' })
```

input:
---
title: Search
description: Search across the sidebar tree and current page structure.
---

## Sidebar search

The sidebar search indexes the rendered navigation tree rather than a separate bespoke search structure. That keeps filtering, expansion, and highlighting in sync.

## Search behavior

Matching pages and headings stay visible. Parent groups stay open so you can see where a hit lives. Sibling pages and sibling headings are hidden, so the filtered tree stays short.

Words longer than 3 characters in the query are highlighted in matching titles and headings.

When search is active, **Search with AI chat** sits at the top of the sidebar so you can send the query to the assistant without scrolling.

## Keyboard support

Arrow keys move through search results and `Enter` jumps to the highlighted item. Escape clears the current search query.

## Group dimming

Top-level group labels should dim too when an entire section has no visible matches, so the whole sidebar reflects the same search state.

name: example/src/selectors.mdx
input:
---
title: Selectors
description: How to target elements on a page using CSS selectors, ARIA refs, and text matchers.
icon: crosshair
---

Playwriter supports three selector strategies for targeting elements. Each has trade-offs between precision, readability, and resilience to DOM changes.

## CSS selectors

Standard CSS selectors work for any element. Use them when you have stable class names or data attributes.

```ts
await page.locator('button.submit-btn').click()
await page.locator('[data-testid="login-form"]').fill('user@example.com')
```

CSS selectors are fast but brittle when class names change between deploys.

## ARIA refs

ARIA refs use the accessibility tree, which is more stable than DOM structure. Playwriter assigns short ref IDs to interactive elements in snapshots.

```ts
// from a snapshot: aria-ref=e5 points to the "Submit" button
await page.locator('aria-ref=e5').click()
```

ARIA refs change between snapshots but are always correct within a single snapshot cycle.

## Text matchers

Match elements by their visible text content. Best for buttons and links with unique labels.

```ts
await page.locator('text=Sign In').click()
await page.locator('text=Accept cookies').click()
```

Text matchers break when the UI is localized or the copy changes.

## Combining strategies

Chain selectors for precision when a single strategy is ambiguous.

```ts
// CSS + text: button inside a specific form
await page.locator('form#login >> text=Submit').click()
```

## Waiting for elements

All selectors auto-wait for the element to appear and become actionable (visible, enabled, not obscured). The default timeout is 30 seconds.

```ts
// explicit wait with custom timeout
await page.locator('text=Dashboard').waitFor({ timeout: 10000 })
```

## Shadow DOM

Playwriter pierces shadow DOM by default. Selectors reach into shadow roots without any special syntax.

```ts
// targets an element inside a web component's shadow root
await page.locator('my-component >> button.inner').click()
```

## iframes

Use `frame()` to switch into an iframe before selecting elements inside it.

```ts
const frame = page.frame({ url: /checkout/ })
await frame.locator('input[name="card"]').fill('4242424242424242')
```

## Best practices

1. Prefer ARIA refs from snapshots for agent-driven flows
2. Use `data-testid` attributes for stable programmatic selectors
3. Avoid selectors that depend on DOM depth or sibling order
4. Combine text + CSS when text alone matches multiple elements

## Debugging selectors

Run `snapshot({ page })` to get a numbered list of interactive elements. Each element shows its ARIA ref, role, name, and bounding box.

```bash
playwriter -e "snapshot({ page })"
```

The snapshot output looks like this:

```text snapshot output wrap
[e1] button "Menu" (32x32 at 16,16)
[e2] link "Home" (48x20 at 80,18)
[e3] input[type=search] "Search docs..." (240x36 at 200,14)
[e4] button "Sign In" (80x36 at 1200,14)
[e5] link "Getting Started" (120x20 at 40,180)
```

## Performance tips

Avoid broad selectors like `div > div > span` that force the engine to walk the entire DOM tree. Narrow selectors with IDs or data attributes are 10-100x faster on complex pages.

## Selector priority

When multiple elements match, Playwriter picks the first visible, actionable match in DOM order. Use `nth=` to disambiguate.

```ts
// click the second "Delete" button on the page
await page.locator('text=Delete >> nth=1').click()
```

## XPath (escape hatch)

XPath is supported as a last resort for legacy pages with no semantic markup.

```ts
await page.locator('xpath=//table/tbody/tr[3]/td[2]').click()
```

Avoid XPath in new code; it couples tests to exact DOM structure.

## Custom selector engines

Register custom selector engines for domain-specific targeting.

```ts
await page.addSelectorEngine('react', {
  query: (root, selector) => root.querySelector(`[data-reactid="${selector}"]`),
  queryAll: (root, selector) => [...root.querySelectorAll(`[data-reactid="${selector}"]`)],
})

await page.locator('react=component-42').click()
```

name: example/src/sessions.mdx
input:
---
title: Sessions
description: Manage isolated browser sessions for parallel agent workflows.
icon: layers
---

Each Playwriter session is an isolated sandbox with its own tab, cookies, and state. Multiple agents can run sessions in parallel without interference.

## Creating a session

```bash
playwriter session new
# outputs: Session 1 created
```

## Listing sessions

```bash
playwriter session list
```

## Running code in a session

```bash
playwriter -s 1 -e "page.goto('https://example.com')"
```

## Session lifecycle

Sessions persist until explicitly closed or the browser restarts. The extension icon shows green when a session is active.

## Parallel sessions

Run multiple sessions simultaneously for parallel workflows:

```bash
playwriter session new  # Session 1
playwriter session new  # Session 2
playwriter -s 1 -e "page.goto('https://site-a.com')" &
playwriter -s 2 -e "page.goto('https://site-b.com')" &
wait
```

## Session isolation

Each session has its own cookies, localStorage, and IndexedDB. Actions in one session never affect another.

## Closing sessions

```bash
playwriter session close 1
playwriter session close --all
```

name: example/src/snapshots.mdx
input:
---
title: Accessibility snapshots
description: Capture a structured snapshot of interactive elements on the current page.
icon: camera
---

Snapshots are the primary way agents understand page state. A snapshot lists every interactive element with its ARIA role, accessible name, bounding box, and a short ref ID for targeting.

## Taking a snapshot

```ts
const snap = await snapshot({ page })
console.log(snap)
```

## Snapshot format

Each line describes one interactive element:

```text wrap
[e1] button "Menu" (32x32 at 16,16)
[e2] link "Home" (48x20 at 80,18)
[e3] input[type=search] "Search docs..." (240x36 at 200,14)
```

The `[e1]` ref ID is stable within a single snapshot but changes across snapshots.

## Filtering by role

Pass a role filter to reduce noise on complex pages.

```ts
const buttons = await snapshot({ page, role: 'button' })
const links = await snapshot({ page, role: 'link' })
```

## Viewport-only mode

By default, snapshots include all elements in the DOM, even those off-screen. Use `viewport: true` to limit to visible elements.

```ts
const visible = await snapshot({ page, viewport: true })
```

## Diffing snapshots

Compare two snapshots to detect page changes after an action.

```ts
const before = await snapshot({ page })
await page.locator('aria-ref=e4').click()
const after = await snapshot({ page })
const diff = diffSnapshots(before, after)
console.log(diff.added, diff.removed, diff.changed)
```

## Snapshot in CI

Snapshots are deterministic given the same page state. Use them in CI to verify UI structure without pixel-level screenshot comparisons.

## Color tokens

Holocron prefers a shared shadcn-style token layer built around `--background`, `--foreground`, `--accent`, `--muted`, and `--border`.

## Primary color

The simplest customization is setting a brand color in `docs.json`:

```json
{
  "colors": {
    "primary": "#6366f1"
  }
}
```

## Editorial styling

The example site also ships with a narrow editorial content column, subtle borders, and type tokens for prose, headings, captions, and code.

## Keeping one design system

When porting components, keep their class structure if it helps, but map them onto the existing token layer instead of introducing a second color namespace.

name: integration-tests/fixtures/realworld-libretto/cli-reference/exec.mdx
input:
---
title: exec
---

> Execute Playwright TypeScript code against the open browser page.

The `exec` command runs TypeScript Playwright code against a live browser session. Use it to validate selectors, inspect page data, prototype individual steps, and experiment with interactions before encoding them in a workflow file.

```bash theme={null}
npx libretto exec --session debug-example "return await page.url()"
```

### Usage

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Single-line">
    Pass the code as a quoted string argument:

    ```bash  theme={null}
    npx libretto exec --session debug-example "return await page.url()"
    npx libretto exec --session debug-example "return await page.locator('button').count()"
    npx libretto exec --session debug-example "await page.locator('button:has-text(\"Continue\")').click()"
    ```

  </Tab>

  <Tab title="stdin (multi-line)">
    Pipe code into `exec -` for complex or multi-line scripts:

    ```bash  theme={null}
    echo "return await page.url()" | npx libretto exec - --session debug-example
    ```

    ```bash  theme={null}
    cat <<'EOF' | npx libretto exec - --session debug-example
    const rows = await page.locator('table tbody tr').all();
    const data = [];
    for (const row of rows) {
      const cells = await row.locator('td').allTextContents();
      data.push(cells);
    }
    return data;
    EOF
    ```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Available globals

Inside the code you pass to `exec`, these variables are available without any imports:

| Global          | Type                      | Description                                 |
| --------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `page`          | `Page`                    | The active Playwright page                  |
| `context`       | `BrowserContext`          | The browser context for the session         |
| `browser`       | `Browser`                 | The browser instance                        |
| `state`         | `Record<string, unknown>` | A mutable object scoped to this `exec` call |
| `fetch`         | `typeof fetch`            | The global fetch function                   |
| `Buffer`        | `typeof Buffer`           | Node.js `Buffer`                            |
| `networkLog`    | `function`                | Read captured network log entries           |
| `actionLog`     | `function`                | Read captured action log entries            |
| `console`       | `Console`                 | Standard console (`log`, `warn`, `error`)   |
| `setTimeout`    | `function`                | Schedule a callback after a delay           |
| `setInterval`   | `function`                | Schedule a repeating callback               |
| `clearTimeout`  | `function`                | Cancel a scheduled `setTimeout`             |
| `clearInterval` | `function`                | Cancel a scheduled `setInterval`            |
| `URL`           | `typeof URL`              | The WHATWG `URL` constructor                |

### Flags

<ParamField path="code" type="string" required>
  The Playwright TypeScript code to execute, passed as the first positional
  argument. Pass `-` to read from stdin.
</ParamField>

<ParamField path="--session" type="string" required>
  The session to execute against.
</ParamField>

<ParamField path="--page" type="string">
  Target a specific page ID within the session. Use `npx libretto pages --session <name>` to list page IDs when a popup or new tab is open.
</ParamField>

<ParamField path="--visualize" type="boolean">
  Enable ghost cursor and highlight visualization. Shows a visible cursor trace
  and element highlights as Playwright interacts with the page.
</ParamField>

### Return values

If the code returns a value, `exec` prints it to stdout:

- Strings are printed as-is.
- All other values are printed as pretty-printed JSON.
- If the code returns nothing (`undefined`), `exec` prints `Executed successfully`.

```bash theme={null}
npx libretto exec --session debug-example "return await page.title()"
# My Page Title

npx libretto exec --session debug-example "return await page.locator('li').count()"
# 12
```

### Rules

<Warning>
  **Let failures throw.** Do not hide `exec` failures with `try/catch` or
  `.catch()`. Swallowed errors make debugging harder. Surface them so you can
  see exactly what failed.
</Warning>

<Warning>
  **Do not run multiple `exec` commands in parallel.** Each `exec` call drives
  the same browser page. Running them concurrently causes race conditions.
</Warning>

- Use `exec` for focused inspection and short-lived interaction experiments.
- Use `exec -` (stdin) for complex multi-line scripts.
- Validate a selector with `exec` before encoding it in a workflow file.
- Use `exec` to prototype a single step, then move the working code into your `.ts` workflow file.

### Examples

```bash theme={null}
# Return the current URL
npx libretto exec --session debug-example "return await page.url()"

# Count how many buttons are on the page
npx libretto exec --session debug-example "return await page.locator('button').count()"

# Click a button
npx libretto exec --session debug-example "await page.locator('button:has-text(\"Continue\")').click()"

# Read a value from an input field
npx libretto exec --session debug-example "return await page.locator('input[name=\"email\"]').inputValue()"

# Run against a named session
npx libretto exec --session debug-example "return await page.url()"

# Run against a specific page in a session
npx libretto exec --session debug-example --page <page-id> "return await page.url()"

# Pipe from stdin (multi-line, named session)
echo "return await page.url()" | npx libretto exec - --session debug-example
```

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="snapshot" icon="camera" href="./snapshot">
    Use snapshot to identify selectors before running exec.
  </Card>

  <Card title="run & resume" icon="play" href="./run-and-resume">
    Move validated exec code into a workflow file and run it end to end.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

name: integration-tests/fixtures/realworld-libretto/cli-reference/open-and-connect.mdx
input:
---
title: open & connect
---

> Launch a browser session or attach to an existing Chrome DevTools Protocol endpoint.

### open

The `open` command launches a browser and navigates to a URL, creating a new named session. It is the starting point for any interactive workflow: once a session is open, `exec`, `snapshot`, and `pages` all work against it.

```bash theme={null}
npx libretto open https://example.com
npx libretto open https://example.com --headless --session debug-example
```

#### When to use `open`

- At the start of script authoring when you need live page state to decide how the workflow should work.
- When the user needs to log in manually before automation begins (use `--headed`).
- Any time you need a fresh, isolated browser instance on a specific URL.

#### Flags

<ParamField path="url" type="string" required>
  The URL to open. Passed as the first positional argument.
</ParamField>

<ParamField path="--headed" type="boolean">
  Run the browser in headed (visible) mode. This is the default when neither
  flag is passed.
</ParamField>

<ParamField path="--headless" type="boolean">
  Run the browser in headless mode. Useful for automated runs that don't need a
  visible window.
</ParamField>

<ParamField path="--session" type="string">
  Name for this session. If omitted, Libretto generates a unique name
  automatically. Use a consistent name to target the session with later
  commands.
</ParamField>

<ParamField path="--viewport" type="string">
  Viewport size in `WIDTHxHEIGHT` format, for example `1920x1080`. Falls back to
  the value in `.libretto/config.json`, then `1366x768`.
</ParamField>

<ParamField path="--provider, -p" type="string">
  Browser provider to use. One of `local`, `kernel`, or `browserbase`. Defaults to `local`.

**Resolution order:** `--provider` flag → `LIBRETTO_PROVIDER` env var → `provider` field in `.libretto/config.json` → `"local"`.

</ParamField>

<Note>
  If a saved auth profile exists for the URL's domain, `open` automatically
  loads it, injecting the saved cookies and localStorage into the new session
  before navigating. You can override this by passing `--auth-profile`
  explicitly, or skip profile loading by not having a saved profile for that
  domain.
</Note>

#### Examples

```bash theme={null}
# Open in headed mode (default)
npx libretto open https://example.com --headed

# Open in headless mode with an explicit session name
npx libretto open https://example.com --headless --session debug-example

# Open with a custom viewport
npx libretto open https://example.com --viewport 1440x900 --session my-session

# Open for a manual login flow, then save the session
npx libretto open https://linkedin.com --headed --session app-login
# ... user logs in ...
npx libretto save linkedin.com --session app-login
```

---

### Cloud browser providers

By default, `open` launches a local Chromium instance. You can instead run the browser in the cloud using the `--provider` flag (or `LIBRETTO_PROVIDER` env var, or `provider` in `.libretto/config.json`).

#### Available providers

| Provider                 | Value         | Required environment variables                  |
| ------------------------ | ------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Local Chromium (default) | `local`       | None                                            |
| Kernel                   | `kernel`      | `KERNEL_API_KEY`                                |
| Browserbase              | `browserbase` | `BROWSERBASE_API_KEY`, `BROWSERBASE_PROJECT_ID` |

#### Configuration

You can set the provider in three ways (highest precedence first):

1. **CLI flag:** `--provider kernel` (or `-p kernel`)
2. **Environment variable:** `LIBRETTO_PROVIDER=kernel`
3. **Config file:** add `"provider": "kernel"` to `.libretto/config.json`

If none is set, the default is `local`.

#### Examples

```bash theme={null}
# Open with Kernel cloud browser
export KERNEL_API_KEY="your-key"
npx libretto open https://example.com --provider kernel

# Open with Browserbase
export BROWSERBASE_API_KEY="your-key"
export BROWSERBASE_PROJECT_ID="your-project-id"
npx libretto open https://example.com -p browserbase

# Set provider via config so you don't need the flag every time
# .libretto/config.json: { "version": 1, "provider": "kernel" }
npx libretto open https://example.com
```

<Note>
  Cloud providers ignore `--headed` / `--headless` and `--viewport` flags since
  the browser runs remotely. The session is always headless from the local
  machine's perspective.
</Note>

---

### connect

The `connect` command attaches to an existing Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) endpoint rather than launching a new browser. Use it to drive a browser that is already running, for example one started with `--remote-debugging-port`, an Electron application, or any other CDP-compatible target.

```bash theme={null}
npx libretto connect http://127.0.0.1:9222 --session my-session
npx libretto connect ws://127.0.0.1:9223 --session another-session
```

#### When to use `connect`

- You have an existing browser process you want to automate without restarting it.
- You are driving an Electron app exposed over CDP.
- You want to attach to a remote browser in a CI environment that has already navigated to the right state.

#### Flags

<ParamField path="cdp-url" type="string" required>
  The CDP endpoint URL to connect to. This can be either an HTTP or WebSocket
  URL and is passed as the first positional argument. Example:
  `http://127.0.0.1:9222`.
</ParamField>

<ParamField path="--session" type="string">
  Name for this session. Recommended to set explicitly when using `connect` so
  you can reference it later.
</ParamField>

#### After connecting

Once connected, all session-scoped commands work normally against the attached browser:

- `exec`: run Playwright TypeScript code
- `snapshot`: capture a screenshot and analyze the page
- `pages`: list open pages

<Warning>
  Libretto does **not** manage the lifecycle of a connected process. Running `npx libretto close --session <name>` clears the Libretto session record but does **not** terminate the remote browser or Electron app.
</Warning>

#### Examples

```bash theme={null}
# Attach to a Chrome instance started with --remote-debugging-port
npx libretto connect http://127.0.0.1:9222 --session chrome-debug

# Inspect the attached page
npx libretto snapshot \
  --session chrome-debug \
  --objective "What is the current page state?" \
  --context "Just attached to a running browser."

# Run code against it
npx libretto exec --session chrome-debug "return await page.url()"
```

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="exec" icon="code" href="./exec">
    Execute Playwright TypeScript against the open page.
  </Card>

  <Card title="snapshot" icon="camera" href="./snapshot">
    Capture a screenshot and analyze page state.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

> List open browser tabs in a session and target specific pages.

### pages

The `pages` command lists all open pages (tabs) in a session and prints their IDs and URLs.

```bash theme={null}
npx libretto pages --session debug-example
```

#### When to use `pages`

- A popup or new tab opened during navigation or interaction.
- `exec` or `snapshot` fails because more than one page is open in the session.
- You are not sure which page holds the relevant state.

After running `pages`, pass the target page ID to other commands with `--page <page-id>`:

```bash theme={null}
# List pages
npx libretto pages --session debug-example

# Target a specific page
npx libretto exec --session debug-example --page <page-id> "return await page.url()"
npx libretto snapshot --session debug-example --page <page-id> \
  --objective "Find the active form" \
  --context "A modal opened in a new tab."
```

#### Flags

<ParamField path="--session" type="string" required>
  The session to list pages for.
</ParamField>
